Session outline (about 60 minutes)
- 0–10 min: Dynamic warm-up and activation
  - Diaphragmatic breathing with abdominal brace: 2 x 5 breaths
  - Cat-cow: 8–10 reps
  - Hip hinge drill (with dowel or broomstick to cue neutral spine): 8–10 reps
  - Glute bridge: 2 x 12
  - Band lateral walks or bodyweight clamshells: 2 x 10 each side
  - Light cardio ramp (bike or brisk walk): 3 minutes, easy

- 10–30 min: Strength Circuit A (lower-body, back-sparing)
  Perform 3 rounds, 60–75 sec rest between exercises, 90 sec between rounds. RPE 6–7/10.
  - Box or goblet squat to bench/chair (dumbbell or kettlebell at chest): 8–12 reps
  - Hip hinge pattern: choose 1
    - Romanian deadlift with light dumbbells, or
    - Hip thrust (bench-supported), or
    - Cable pull-through
    8–12 reps
  - Step-up (knee height box) or split squat: 8–10 reps each leg
  Cues: brace core before each rep, keep neutral spine, hinge from hips, avoid rounding.

- 30–42 min: Low-impact cardio intervals
  Choose bike, elliptical, or incline treadmill walk.
  - 6 rounds of 45 sec hard (RPE 7–8/10) + 75 sec easy (RPE 3–4/10)
  - 2 min easy cool-down at the end

- 42–57 min: Strength Circuit B (upper + core stability)
  Perform 2–3 rounds, 45–60 sec rest between exercises. RPE 6–7/10.
  - Incline push-up (hands on bench) or dumbbell floor press: 8–12 reps
  - One-arm supported dumbbell row (knee/hand on bench): 10–12 reps each side
  - Anti-rotation core: Pallof press (cable or band): 10–12 reps each side
  - McGill core “Big Three”
    - Modified curl-up: 8–10 reps with 5-sec holds
    - Side plank (knees or feet): 15–30 sec each side
    - Bird-dog: 6–8 reps each side with 3-sec holds

- 57–60 min: Cool-down and mobility
  - Easy walk or cycling: 2 min
  - Gentle stretches: hip flexor, glute/piriformis, calves; 20–30 sec each
  Keep stretches pain-free; avoid aggressive forward flexion.

Weekly structure and progression
- Frequency: 3x/week for this session. On 2 additional days, do 20–30 min low-impact Zone 2 cardio (RPE 4–5/10) or a brisk walk.
- Progression (each week if pain-free and form solid):
  - Add 1–2 reps per set up to top of rep range, then increase weight 2–5% and drop reps back down.

- “Brace, then move”: light abdominal brace before each rep.
- Neutral spine: no rounding or excessive arching; hinge at hips.
- Pain rule: stop or regress if pain exceeds 3/10 or radiates; consult a clinician or physical therapist if symptoms persist or worsen.

This is general guidance; if you haven’t had recent clearance for exercise with hypertension, check with your healthcare provider first. Stop immediately if you feel chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness, or severe knee pain.

How each 30‑minute session is structured
- Warm‑up (5 minutes): gentle marching in place, arm circles, shoulder rolls, ankle pumps, hip hinges. Aim for easy pace you can comfortably chat through.
- Main work (20 minutes): follow the day’s template below.
- Cool‑down (5 minutes): slow walk/march, calf/hamstring/quadriceps/hip flexor stretches, deep breathing.

Intensity guide
- Use the talk test/RPE: keep most cardio at RPE 4–6 (you can talk in short sentences, not sing).
- Strength: light to moderate loads where last 2 reps feel challenging but you can maintain form and breathe normally.

Three workout templates (rotate through the week)
1) Low‑impact cardio intervals (knee‑friendly)
- 10 x 1 minute brisk + 1 minute easy (total 20 min)
- Brisk options: fast marching, side‑steps with a mini band above knees, low step‑touch to a sturdy low step, shadow boxing (no jumping), mini high‑knees to a pain‑free height, or stationary cycling if available.
- Easy options: slow march, gentle step‑touch, slow shadow boxing.
- Cues: keep knees soft, land quietly, avoid twisting pivots. If anything spikes knee pain above 3/10, substitute seated marching or seated shadow boxing.

2) Strength circuit A (full body, knee‑friendly focus)
- Do 2 rounds in Week 1–2, then 3 rounds starting Week 3. Work 40 seconds, rest 20 seconds between moves.
- Exercises:
  - Hip hinge/RDL with dumbbells (light): hinge at hips, slight knee bend.
  - Seated or wall row with resistance band: squeeze shoulder blades.
  - Box/chair squat to a comfortable depth: sit back to a chair, stand up; use light dumbbell goblet hold if comfortable.
  - Standing overhead press with light dumbbells: exhale as you press, avoid breath‑holding.
  - Glute bridge on mat: squeeze glutes, keep knees aligned.
  - Dead bug or bird‑dog for core: slow, controlled breathing.
- Keep breathing; exhale on effort. Skip or lighten overhead presses if BP or neck/shoulder discomfort rises.

3) Strength circuit B + cardio finisher
- Circuit (same structure as A):
  - Step‑back supported split squat to a chair (very shallow, use wall/chair for balance). If knee discomfort, replace with sit‑to‑stand.
  - Band pull‑apart or band face pull.
  - Incline wall or counter push‑ups.
  - Banded lateral walks (mini band above knees, short steps).
  - Standing calf raises holding onto support.
- Finisher (5 minutes): very easy cardio (march or walk) to cool intensity, not breathless.

Weekly schedule (30 minutes per day)
- Day 1: Low‑impact cardio intervals
- Day 2: Strength circuit A
- Day 3: Mobility + easy cardio
  - Main 20 minutes: gentle flow—cat‑cow, thoracic rotations, hip flexor stretch, hamstring stretch, ankle mobility, banded external rotations, 8–10 minute easy walk/march.
- Day 4: Low‑impact cardio intervals
- Day 5: Strength circuit B + easy 3–5 minute cardio at end if time
- Day 6: Recovery cardio + mobility
  - 20 minutes continuous easy walk/march/cycle at conversational pace + 5 minutes of stretches.
- Day 7: Rest or gentle yoga/stretching (optional 10–15 minute easy walk if you feel good)

Progression over 4 weeks
- Week 1: Learn movements, RPE 4–5. Strength circuits 2 rounds.
- Week 2: Add one more interval to cardio (e.g., 11 rounds of 1 on/1 off) or extend brisk segments to 75 seconds. Keep strength at 2 rounds or increase a few exercises to 3 rounds if form is solid.
- Week 3: Slightly increase dumbbell weight or band tension; all strength circuits 3 rounds. Cardio intervals RPE 5–6.
- Week 4: Lengthen brisk intervals to 90 seconds with 60 seconds easy, or keep 1/1 and add a 5‑minute steady cooldown walk for extra volume.

Knee‑pain safeguards
- Favor hinges (RDLs) and shallow squats to a box over deep knee flexion. Keep knees tracking over toes; avoid knees caving inward.
- No jumping or fast pivots. Step height low. If pain >3/10 or lingers >24 hours, reduce range, load, or swap exercise.
- Strengthen hips/glutes (bridges, lateral walks, clamshells) to offload knees.

Hypertension safety tips
- Warm up and cool down every session. Avoid sudden position changes; rise slowly from the floor.
- Do not hold your breath (avoid the Valsalva). Exhale on the effort for every rep.
- Prefer continuous or interval cardio at moderate intensity; avoid all‑out sprints initially.
- Limit long isometric holds; keep planks to 10–20 seconds with easy breathing if included.
- If you monitor BP at home, train when you feel well and your readings are in your usual controlled range. If you experience dizziness, unusual headache, chest pain, or vision changes, stop and seek medical guidance.

Quick equipment guide
- Dumbbells: start light; when you can complete all sets with perfect form and RPE <4, increase 2–5 lb per hand.
- Bands: choose tension that challenges last 2 reps while maintaining form.
- Mat: use for floor core/glute work; if getting up/down is uncomfortable, do seated variations.

Optional checks and tracking
- Keep a simple log: session type, RPE, knee pain (0–10), and how you felt 2 hours later and the next morning.
- Aim for 6,000–8,000+ daily steps on non‑workout time if feasible; increase gradually.

Hi Emily—thanks for sharing. I’m not a medical professional, but I can offer general guidance and help you think about next steps.

A few quick questions to better understand what you’re experiencing:
- How often do the panic attacks occur, how long do they last, and what symptoms do you feel (e.g., heart racing, chest tightness, dizziness)?
- Do you notice common triggers (caffeine, stress, crowded places)?
- Are you avoiding activities because of fear of another attack?
- Any current medications, supplements, or recent changes (including caffeine or alcohol)?
- If you ever feel in immediate danger or have thoughts of harming yourself, please seek urgent help right away.

Coping strategies you can try during anxiety or a panic surge:
- Slow breathing: inhale through your nose for 4 seconds, hold 2–4, exhale slowly through your mouth for 6–8; repeat for a few minutes.
- Grounding (5-4-3-2-1): name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.
- Gentle muscle release: drop your shoulders, unclench jaw, relax hands; scan and release tension.
- Brief movement: a short walk or light exercise to discharge adrenaline.
- Reduce stimulants: avoid caffeine/nicotine when you’re anxious, and limit overall intake.

Day-to-day steps that can help:
- Keep a simple log of attacks (time, trigger, symptoms, what helped) to spot patterns.
- Prioritize sleep, regular meals, and consistent activity.
- Create a “panic plan” card with a breathing routine and a reassuring statement (e.g., “This is uncomfortable but not dangerous; it will pass.”).

When to seek professional care:
- If attacks are new, worsening, or include severe chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath, get medical evaluation to rule out physical causes.
- Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety and panic; consider a therapist or discussing options with your primary care clinician. They can also discuss medications if appropriate.

If you need immediate support, contact local emergency services. In the US you can call/text 988 for 24/7 support; in the UK, Samaritans at 116 123.
